turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thank you. Um... well, I came in because things are just getting really, really out of hand lately. I feel like I absolutely cannot get my schoolwork and my little accessories shop organized at the same time. It's just... it's impossible. I run this tiny shop online making hair clips and jewelry and stuff, which I love, but my room is literally a disaster zone right now. 

Between the shop and my classes, everything is just colliding. My supplies—like all the beads and wire and shipping mailers—and then my school due dates, all my business receipts, my assignment notes... they all just end up in these huge, overwhelming piles. Like, everywhere. On my desk, on my floor, on my bed. I'll have a receipt for resin right next to a sticky note about a history essay, and I look at it all and I just... I don't know what to do first. I'll sit there and think, 'Okay, I need to study,' but then I see an unfinished necklace, and then I remember I have to mail a package, and I just end up moving the piles from my bed to my chair so I can sleep, and then from my chair back to my bed the next morning. It’s exhausting, honestly, and I just can't seem to figure out how people keep all these things straight without completely losing their minds.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot get their schoolwork and accessories shop organized, resulting in overwhelming piles of supplies and notes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted from their intended task of studying by seeing an unfinished necklace or remembering another task.

turns.doctor_question: When you try to clean up, do you find it hard to throw things away or part with items?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, no, it’s definitely not that. Like, I’m not attached to the trash or anything! If a piece of wire is too short or a bead is chipped or I have empty packaging, I have zero problem tossing it. Actually, it’s almost the opposite? Like, when I finally get that sudden burst of energy to clean—which usually happens at, like, 2 AM when I should definitely be sleeping—I go into this crazy overdrive mode. I'll grab a huge black trash bag and just start chucking things. I’m like, 'Get it out, get it all out!' 

But the problem is, I move so fast that I don't really pay attention. Just last week, I was doing one of my late-night purges because the pile on my chair got too high and I knocked it over, and I ended up throwing away a super important invoice for my resin supplier. I didn't even realize it until three days later when I was looking for it everywhere, tearing my room apart all over again. So, no, parting with stuff isn't the issue at all. I don't hold onto empty boxes or wrappers or anything like that. 

It's just the sorting part. Like, if I have a pile of perfectly good jewelry clasps mixed with my history notes, I can't throw *those* away, obviously, because I need them, but figuring out where to put them... that's where my brain just completely short-circuits. I'll pick up a clasp, think about the necklace I was making, go to find the chain for it, realize the chain is tangled, sit down on the floor to start untangling it, and then an hour later my room is actually messier than when I started because I pulled out three more boxes of supplies. So yeah, throwing things away is totally fine, I just... I can't do the putting-things-in-their-proper-place part. It's like my brain just skips that step entirely.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes making careless mistakes due to not paying attention, such as accidentally throwing away a super important invoice.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states having difficulty with sorting and putting things in their proper place, describing how their brain 'short-circuits' during organization.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily sidetracked while trying to clean, moving from picking up a clasp to looking for a chain to untangling it, leaving the room messier than before.

turns.doctor_question: Did you experience similar difficulties with attention and keeping things organized when you were a child, such as in elementary school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, yeah, absolutely. It’s actually kind of funny you ask that, because my mom was just talking about this the other day when I was complaining to her about my room. She actually still has a whole file folder of my old report cards and notes from my teachers from back when I was in elementary school—like, first through fourth grade, mostly. And it's basically the exact same story, just, you know, without the jewelry shop part. 

Like, she was reading some of them to me, and every single teacher wrote almost the exact same thing. It was always, 'She has so much trouble staying in her seat,' or 'She needs constant reminders to stay at her desk.' I guess I was always popping up to go sharpen a pencil, or look out the window, or see what the kid three desks down was doing. And the talking! Oh my gosh, the talking. The notes always said I was blurting out answers before the teacher even finished the question, or just talking over people without raising my hand. I wasn't trying to be rude or anything, I just... I’d get the thought in my head and it just had to come out right that second, you know? Like I couldn't hold it in if I tried. 

And group work was apparently a total disaster. The notes said I would just completely rush through whatever activity we were doing. Like, I understood the material fine—I was actually pretty good at reading and math back then—but I would just speed through it so fast, barely looking at the instructions, just trying to get to the end because I was already bored of it. I'd finish in five minutes and then start bothering the other kids who were still trying to work. My mom said she used to dread parent-teacher conferences because it was always the same conversation about how I needed to 'slow down' and 'think before I act' and 'stay in my designated area.' So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing. It’s just that back then it was my desk at school, and now it’s my entire life and my business.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions rushing through activities and barely looking at the instructions.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports that teachers noted she had trouble staying in her seat and was always popping up.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states she had issues with excessive talking in class.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient confirms she would blurt out answers before the teacher finished the question.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes talking over people without raising her hand and bothering other kids who were trying to work.
